spellingsNote:
**One basis, stated: England Births & Baptisms 1538-1975 on FindMyPast, searched nationally, every form asked the same way.** 27 spellings tried, 20 productive, **373 index entries** between 1565 and 1909 — and that is a floor, not a total. **SINIGOR and SINNIGER were added on the evening of 21 September**, found by a single wildcard query over eleven years of one county, hours after the table had been rebuilt and called complete.

**The column counts entries, not children.** On 21 September the five largest forms were read row by row and counted as events rather than as rows: **about one entry in six is a repeat**, and the repetition sits almost wholly in SANIGER and SANIGAR, whose parishes were transcribed more than once. **The measured figures are on [/spellings](/spellings/)**, where they are derived from the count rather than written out again here.

This replaces a table of nineteen forms whose counts were entries in the parish registers read for this archive — a narrower and differently-drawn source. **Those counts were not wrong; they were not comparable**, which is why SANIGOR and SYNIGAR could not simply be added to them when they were found. The old table is kept in the data as `spellingsOld` rather than deleted.

**SANYGER and SYNIGER still count nought**, which is the finding that survived the change of basis: they are the 1608 muster's forms, in Smyth's Men and Armour and in no register anywhere. **SANIGRE counts nought here too and is in the table anyway** — it is the only form under which Thomas Sinegar's 1828 marriage is indexed, and a spelling that is invisible in one set and decisive in another is exactly what this table exists to show. **SINGER and SANGER are excluded** — 127 and 40 in Gloucestershire alone, and they are ordinary English surnames rather than forms of this one; counting them would drown the table in strangers.

grsi.head: Twenty-four deaths, with the register and the entry number
grsi.lede: The Gloucestershire Registration Service and the Gloucestershire Family History Society between them have indexed the registrars' own books and put them online free. It is not the GRO index: it gives the LOCAL register and entry number, which is what a certificate is ordered against.
grsi.coverage: Coverage checked before the search, not after. For deaths the districts that matter are complete: Thornbury/Berkeley 1837–1948, Dursley 1837–1937 (20 registers), Wotton-under-Edge 1837–1937 (19 registers), Uley 1837–1906.

lydia.head: And the one that was being looked for
lydia.body: LYDIA SANIGAR, died 1851, register 3, entry 265. This archive has wanted her since it began: she is the Lyddya Sinegar aged seventy in Hannah's house in 1841, and she is the wife whose maiden surname the marriage of about 1797 would give.
lydia.careful: The index gives a year, a register and an entry — not a date, an age, an abode or a maiden name. It locates the certificate; it does not replace it. What it does do is make the certificate orderable against the local register rather than the GRO index.

spelling.head: A spelling hid her, for the fourth time
spelling.body: Searched as SANIGER, the 1849–1853 window returns two people and neither is Lydia. Searched as SANIGAR it returns three, and she is the second. The surname box does prefix matching when Exact Match is left unticked, so the only safe search for this family is the stem SANIG — which returns all five.
spelling.means: Hannah's baptism was hidden under SANIGOR. Her brother's marriage was hidden under SANIGRE. The Sussex sisters were hidden under ARCY. Lydia's death was hidden under SANIGAR. The pattern is now four for four, and it is the single most reliable fact about researching this family.

marriages.head: Ten marriages, with the other name
marriages.note: The marriage index gives both partners, which the GRO quarterly index does not do for this period without a second lookup.
marriages.oddity: One entry appears twice under one reference, C7/1168 in 1858, with the bride as both Caroline STOCKWELL and Caroline WORKMAN. One event, two surnames for the same woman — a remarriage, a step-parent's name, or an index error. It is left exactly as the index gives it.

births.head: Twenty-seven births
births.note: The birth search accepts a MOTHER'S MAIDEN NAME as a search term, which is the field that turns an index into a family. It is not displayed in results, but it can be searched against — so a maiden name guessed from a marriage can be tested against a birth.

lives.head: What the three indexes do together
lives.body: Read across, births and deaths in the same index start closing on each other. Nine names appear in both, at intervals that read as short lives:
lives.and: EMILY SOPHIA, born 1851, marries Robert Dore in 1879. ALBERT THOMAS, born 1863, marries Ellen Kate Young in 1891. ARTHUR EDWARD, born 1865, marries Louisa Powell in 1891, a fortnight or so from his brother by the look of the references — 34 No 1154 and 34 No 1168.
lives.chip: matched on name and date, not on a document
lives.careful: Every one of these joins is an inference. The index gives a surname, a forename, a year and a register reference, and nothing that proves the Catharine born in 1848 is the Catharine who died in 1849. In a district where the same dozen forenames repeat for a century, that is a real risk. They are set out because they say where to spend certificate money, not because they are established.

freebmd.head: The same three deaths, in the other index
freebmd.lede: The table above is the LOCAL register — the registrar's own book, register and entry number. FreeBMD indexes the GRO's quarterly volumes instead, which is a different index of the same events. Searched on 15 September, it carries all three of the Thornbury deaths this archive cares about, and gives the reference a GRO certificate is ordered against.
freebmd.means: Two indexes, built from different books by different people, agree on three deaths in the same district within twenty-one months. The pairing of local entry to GRO volume is an IDENTIFICATION — same name, same district, same year — not a proven match, because neither index names a parent, an age or an address. What it does settle is that Lydia can now be ordered from the GRO as well as from Gloucester.
freebmd.controlHead: And the control that made the null meaningful
freebmd.control: FreeBMD's first three answers here were NOUGHT, and all three were false. A search across 1837–1875 returns nothing at all — the form silently refuses a range that wide and redisplays itself, which looks exactly like an empty result. The control was CHARLOTTE DARCY, whose death this archive already holds from the GRO index: searched for 1869 alone she comes back «Darcy Charlotte 73 Brighton 2b 152», the reference this site already carried. Narrowing the Sanigar search to three years then produced all three deaths at once.
